articleHeadline: El peligroso hongo que "transmiten los gatos" ya infectó a más de 11.000 personas en este país de Latinoamérica
articleSummary: Sporothrix brasiliensis, a zoonotic fungus transmitted from cats, originated in Brazil and has raised alarms across Uruguay and much of South America. The Uruguayan Institute of Hygiene confirmed cases in Maldonado and Rocha, signaling a shift in the regional epidemiology and prompting reinforced surveillance. The World Health Organization notes that in South American areas affected by this species—primarily Brazil—more than 11,000 human cases have been reported in the past decade. Transmission occurs through direct contact with infected cats, especially strays or animals with visible lesions. In felines, facial, muzzle, and paw ulcers are common and lesions with crusts facilitate transmission via scratches or bites to humans. In people, infections begin as skin and subcutaneous nodules, often along lymphatic channels; most are cutaneous but lymph nodes can be involved, requiring prolonged therapy. Early medical evaluation improves prognosis. Sporothrix brasiliensis is thermally dimorphic: filamentous at 25°C and yeast-like at 37°C.
notes: ブラジル原産のSporothrix brasiliensisがウルグアイ（MaldonadoとRocha）で確認され、地域疫学の変化を示唆。過去10年で南米で11,000例以上報告。猫（特に野良猫）からの直接接触で感染。皮膚・皮下結節、リンパ節病変を形成し長期治療が必要。WHOが言及しており国際的な関心事項。

articleSummary: As of 13 March 2026, a Vietnamese clinician from the Ho Chi Minh City University of Medicine and Pharmacy Hospital warns that botulism poisoning results from Clostridium botulinum in foods improperly processed or preserved. The bacteria thrive in anaerobic, sealed or naturally fermented environments. Common sources include fermented fish, salted or cured fish, other fermented meats, homemade canned foods, pâté, sausages, smoked meats, and pickled vegetables produced without hygiene. Ingestion of botulinum toxin can cause severe neurologic illness, starting with facial weakness, progressing to limb paralysis and possibly respiratory failure; death may occur without prompt treatment. Prevention focuses on safe preparation and storage: correct salt concentrations and fermentation times, discard bulging or foul-smelling cans, and ensure thorough cooking of homemade preserved items to inactivate toxin. Antitoxin therapy exists but is scarce and often imported from WHO or centers in Vietnam.
notes: この記事は「Doctor 24/7」という医療情報シリーズの一部で、ホーチミン市医科薬科大学病院の臨床医による一般的な健康教育コンテンツ。特定のボツリヌス中毒発生事例や症例数の報告は含まれておらず、食品の適切な保存方法や症状の認識、予防策に関する啓発情報のみ。WHOや国内センターから抗毒素を輸入する必要があることへの言及はあるが、現在進行中の健康事象を示すものではない。

articleSummary: Indonesia ranks second worldwide in measles cases, reporting 10,744 cases, behind Yemen with 11,288, per the Indonesian Pediatric Association (IDAI). The rise correlates with declines in routine measles vaccination coverage as many parents remain hesitant or afraid to vaccinate their children. Dr. Piprim Basarah Yanuarso, IDAI chair, warns measles can cause serious complications—pneumonia, severe diarrhea with dehydration, otitis leading to hearing loss, and encephalitis—especially in malnourished or immunocompromised children. Measles is highly contagious, with an estimated basic reproduction number of 12–18, making herd immunity difficult to sustain unless vaccination coverage stays above 95%. articleHeadline: Dengue e a vacina que pode mudar essa história
articleSummary: Brazil faces annual dengue waves as Aedes aegypti multiplies with rain; 2024 recorded over 4 million probable dengue cases, thousands of hospitalizations, and hundreds of deaths, stressing emergency services in major capitals. The four serotypes enable reinfection and immune-enhancement, raising severe-disease risk. Vector control remains essential but insufficient alone to curb epidemics. Two vaccines offer a turning point. Takeda’s Qdenga is a two-dose vaccine (three-month interval) with moderate efficacy against dengue and strong protection against hospitalization; it’s being rolled out in Brazil for select groups, especially children and adolescents. More transformative is Butantan’s tetravalent, single-dose vaccine, protecting against all four serotypes. Clinical trials in Brazil with over 16,000 volunteers show global efficacy above 70% against symptomatic dengue and higher protection against severe disease and hospitalizations. If scaled through the public program, it could markedly reduce cases and hospital pressure over the coming decade, though rollout will take years, not immediate elimination.

articleSummary: Oropouche fever is rising in Minas Gerais, Brazil, with a 378% increase from 2024 to 2025. articleHeadline: First-Trimester Oropouche Linked to Brain Malformations
articleSummary: Five confirmed cases of vertical transmission of Oropouche virus in Brazil (Pernambuco, Ceará, Acre) are associated with fatal fetal CNS malformations, establishing the virus as an obstetric threat and prompting prenatal protocol changes in endemic areas. Molecular confirmation used RT-PCR to detect viral RNA in placental tissue, umbilical cord blood, amniotic fluid, and fetal brain tissue; an additional 22 fetal deaths remain under investigation. All malformations followed maternal infection in the first trimester, implying a critical window during organogenesis. The phenotype includes severe microcephaly, ventriculomegaly, corpus callosum dysgenesis, posterior fossa abnormalities, intracranial calcifications, arthrogryposis, and ocular changes (microphthalmia, chorioretinal atrophy). Placental histopathology showed necrotizing villitis and deciduitis with viral replication in trophoblastic cells, supporting hematogenous transplacental transmission. Recommendations: multiplex testing for Oropouche, dengue, Zika, chikungunya, and Mayaro; serial neurosonography every 4 weeks; consider fetal MRI; delivery per obstetric guidelines and collection of maternal and neonatal samples at birth for surveillance.

articleSummary: Avian influenza outbreak confirmed in wildlife in the extreme south of Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, with 23 positive detections (coscoroba swan and black-crowned night heron) linked to the Taim Ecological Reserve since late February. Producers and the public are urged to report suspected cases; key signs include respiratory or neurological symptoms and sudden, elevated mortality in birds.

articleHeadline: Campo Grande registra 238 notificações por dengue em 2026; cinco bairros têm alto risco
articleSummary: Campo Grande has registered 238 dengue notifications so far in 2026, with no severe cases or suspected dengue deaths, according to Cievs (Centro de Informações Estratégicas em Vigilância em Saúde). Five neighborhoods—Chácara dos Poderes, Itanhangá, Veraneio, Centenário, and Santo Antônio—show very high transmission risk for Aedes aegypti–related diseases. Twelve dengue patients were treated in primary care, and another 120 were seen in UPAs and CRSs. Although Mato Grosso do Sul leads Brazil in chikungunya incidence in 2026, Campo Grande has reported no chikungunya cases so far this year. In Dourados, the municipality confirmed an outbreak in Indigenous villages; the Ministério da Saúde records one death there and investigates a second in Aquidauana. The dengue incidence rate in Campo Grande is 26.51, with the five neighborhoods above the municipal average. A total of 61.88 liters of insecticide were used; endemic agents visited 29,000 residences and identified breeding in 819.
notes: Campo Grande市では238件の通知があるが重症例・死亡例なし。一方、Dourados市の先住民村落でアウトブレイク確認、1名死亡確定・1名調査中。Mato Grosso do Sul州が2026年ブラジル国内でチクングニア発生率トップだが、Campo Grande市では今年チクングニア例なし。デング熱はブラジルで流行性疾患であり、この規模が異常かどうかは過去データとの比較が必要。現時点では国内対応可能な範囲内と判断されるが、先住民コミュニティでの死亡例調査と流行拡大の推移を注視すべき。

articleHeadline: Measles cases fall to 511 in week 9 after immunization: Ministry
articleSummary: Measles cases in Indonesia fell to 511 in week 9 of 2026, down from 531, due to mass immunization and education campaigns. articleHeadline: Bangladesh steps up watch for drug-resistant malaria in Rohingya camps
articleSummary: Bangladesh will launch its first surveillance study to detect drug-resistant malaria strains in Rohingya refugee camps near the Myanmar border, Cox's Bazar, involving ICDDR,B, the National Malaria Elimination Programme, and BRAC. articleHeadline: Indonesia faces surge in measles cases
articleSummary: Measles surge in Indonesia with 2025 total of 17,204 cases, second-highest global incidence after Yemen according to WHO. articleHeadline: 39 including 14 students taken ill as jaundice spreads in Himachal's Hamirpur
articleSummary: Jaundice outbreak in Hamirpur district, Himachal Pradesh, with 39 people ill, including 14 students from a Swahal government school. Health and Jal Shakti teams collecting water samples; one sample contaminated in preliminary tests; comprehensive analysis underway. Drinking-water supply suspended briefly; residents advised to boil water; chlorine tablets distributed. Investigations point to contaminated water from the local drinking-water scheme; wastewater discharge from nearby factories and restaurant, and bridge construction obstructing stream flow as potential factors. articleSummary: Yellow fever vaccination guidance from Venezuelan health authorities emphasizes vaccination as the best defense, but with important contraindications. Immunocompromised individuals (e.g., HIV or undergoing chemotherapy), children under six months, and those allergic to eggs or vaccine components should not be vaccinated. People over 60 and pregnant women require medical evaluation before vaccination. Vaccination is strongly advised for residents or travelers aged 9 months to 59 years to risk zones, for those needing a vaccination certificate to enter other countries, and for farmers or people in forested areas. Yellow fever presents with abrupt, systemic illness, 3–6 day incubation, and three clinical phases; about 20% progress to a critical phase with a 60% fatality. Clinicians should consider outbreaks and rule out yellow fever in dengue-like cases. Prevention includes bed nets, long sleeves, and eliminating mosquito breeding sites. Travelers should be vaccinated at least 10 days before arrival, especially to Aragua, Barinas, Lara, Portuguesa, or forested areas, amid reactivation in the Amazon basin with broader geographic spread.

articleSummary: Mpox can spread at home through contaminated objects (fomites); the virus can survive on everyday items and porous materials, enabling indirect transmission from infected individuals with skin lesions. Household items with higher risk include towels and bath sponges, sheets, blankets, pillows, personal care items like razors and toothbrushes, and fabric-covered furniture, which may become contaminated with lesion fluids. To reduce transmission, avoid sharing towels, clothing, or utensils; wash clothes and bed linens regularly in hot water; clean surfaces with 70% alcohol; frequently disinfect door handles, tables, and light switches; use disposable gloves when handling contaminated laundry; avoid shaking dirty fabrics; maintain good indoor ventilation. Common mpox symptoms to watch for are sudden fever, severe headache, swollen lymph nodes (neck or groin), marked fatigue, muscle pains, and skin lesions or rash; seek medical care promptly and isolate until evaluated. articleSummary: Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, remains a concern in China; pulmonary TB is most common. In schools, crowded conditions and developing immunity heighten infection risk. TB spreads via airborne droplets; symptoms include cough with sputum, low fever, fatigue, weight loss, and night sweats. Screening aims for early detection of infection or disease to prevent progression and curb campus transmission. Methods include: tuberculin skin test (TST) with 5 IU PPD; interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA) for higher specificity; chest X-ray for radiographic changes; sputum smear and culture; and molecular tests like Xpert MTB/RIF for rapid detection and rifampicin resistance. A multi-dimensional strategy: targeted screening for high-risk students with dynamic health records; entrance examinations using a joint TST/IGRA initial screen plus chest X-ray re-screen; enhanced health education and cross-sector collaboration between education and health authorities. Early, science-based screening protects student health and learning environment.

articleSummary: Sporothrix brasiliensis, a fungus carried by cats that causes sporotrichosis in humans via skin wounds, has triggered a new South American outbreak. As of 2026-03-14, Uruguay reports the latest cluster traced to 2025, involving a family and their pets. The disease, common in tropical and subtropical climates, has affected Brazil and other South American countries. Transmission is cutaneous: cat scratches or bites; direct contact with wounds or secretions; or inhalation of feline secretions. Symptoms include nodules on exposed skin (face, arms, legs); mucosal involvement; and in rare cases deep infections that can cause arthritis, pneumonia, or meningitis. Treatments include oral itraconazole or terbinafine; potassium iodide solutions may be used. Prevention centers on early detection and treatment of infected cats; human treatment can be prolonged, typically 3–4 months. Climate-related factors and flooding may influence outbreaks, per WHO.

articleSummary: Sporothrix brasiliensis, a fungus transmitted from cats to humans, causes skin infections and can lead to chronic sporotrichosis with ulcers on the arms and hands. In Uruguay, the Institute of Hygiene warned of outbreaks linked to a Brazilian-origin fungus, with cases reported in the departments of Maldonado and Rocha, triggering surveillance by the Ministry of Public Health and the Zoonosis Commission. The first case involved a family that adopted a cat later showing fungal signs. The disease tends to cause severe skin lesions, especially in young children and older adults. Infected cats typically have facial, nose, and paw lesions with crusts and hair loss and can spread the fungus to people through scratches, bites, or contact with purulent wound material, which contains high fungal concentrations. The fungus can remain active in feline ulcers, enabling infection through minor skin breaks.
